words.meaning: O you who are worthy of worship

grammar.en: past active participle m. nom. pl.

closing.translation: Om. May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O you who are worthy of worship. Praising you with firm limbs and bodies, may we attain the life that the gods have appointed. May Indra of great fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan who knows all grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya of the unharmed wheel-rim grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati grant us well-being. Om. Peace, peace, peace.
notes: The peace invocation of the Upaniṣads of the Atharvaveda, printed at the opening of the edition. Śaṅkara's Praśna bhāṣya does not comment on it; the translation gives the plain sense of the words.

sanskrit.deva:
अथ हैनं सुकेशा भारद्वाजः पप्रच्छ ।
भगवन्हिरण्यनाभः कौसल्यो राजपुत्रो मामुपेत्यैतं प्रश्नमपृच्छत ।
षोडशकलं भारद्वाज पुरुषं वेत्थ ।
तमहं कुमारमब्रुवं नाहमिमं वेद ।
यद्यहमिममवेदिषं कथं ते नावक्ष्यमिति ।
समूलो वा एष परिशुष्यति योऽनृतमभिवदति ।
तस्मान्नार्हाम्यनृतं वक्तुं ।
स तूष्णीं रथमारुह्य प्रवव्राज ।
तं त्वा पृच्छामि क्वासौ पुरुष इति ॥ १ ॥

padaccheda.deva: अथ ह एनम् सुकेशा भारद्वाजः पप्रच्छ भगवन् हिरण्यनाभः कौसल्यः राज-पुत्रः माम् उपेत्य एतम् प्रश्नम् अपृच्छत षोडश-कलम् भारद्वाज पुरुषम् वेत्थ तम् अहम् कुमारम् अब्रुवम् न अहम् इमम् वेद यदि अहम् इमम् अवेदिषम् कथम् ते न अवक्ष्यम् इति स-मूलः वै एषः परिशुष्यति यः अनृतम् अभिवदति तस्मात् न अर्हामि अनृतम् वक्तुम् सः तूष्णीम् रथम् आरुह्य प्रवव्राज तम् त्वा पृच्छामि क्व असौ पुरुषः इति

translations.text: Then Sukeśan Bhāradvāja asked him: ‘Venerable sir, Hiraṇyanābha, a prince of Kosala, came to me and asked this question: “Bhāradvāja, do you know the Puruṣa of sixteen parts?” I said to that prince: “I do not know him. If I had known him, how would I not have told you? He who speaks what is untrue withers away, root and all; therefore I may not speak what is untrue.” He mounted his chariot in silence and went away. I ask you about him: where is that Puruṣa?’

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the praśna: it has been said that the whole world, made of effects and causes, together with the self whose nature is knowing, comes to rest in deep sleep in the supreme imperishable. By force of that it is settled that at the dissolution also the world rests in that same imperishable and arises from it alone, for an effect cannot come to rest in what is not its cause; and it was said ‘from the Self this prāṇa is born’. That the highest good comes from knowing fully the root of the world is the settled sense of all the Upaniṣads; and it has just been said ‘he, knowing all, becomes all’. It must now be told where that imperishable, the true, called Puruṣa, is to be known: for this the question is begun. The story is told to show how hard the knowledge is to gain, so that those who seek liberation take special pains to gain it.

Śaṅkara: ṣoḍaśakala: he in whom there are sixteen parts, like limbs, whose form is laid on the Self by ignorance. ‘How would I not have told you’: you who have every quality of a pupil and ask for it. Seeing him still unconvinced, he spoke again to convince him: he who, making himself other than he is, speaks what is not as things are, dries up root and all, is cut off from this world and the next. The prince went away in silence, ashamed, as he had come. From this it is settled that one who knows must tell the knowledge to a fit pupil who has come in the right way, and that what is untrue must not be spoken in any condition. ‘I ask you about him’, who stays in my heart like a dart, as something to be known: where is that Puruṣa who is to be known?
The e-text reads kāsau; it is set right here to kvāsau, as the bhāṣya has it.

translations.text: He said to him: ‘Here itself, within the body, dear one, is that Puruṣa in whom these sixteen parts arise.’

notes: Śaṅkara: here within the body, in the space of the lotus of the heart, is that Puruṣa; he is not to be known in some other place. In him the sixteen parts, prāṇa and the rest, arise. Through the sixteen parts, which are adjuncts, the partless Puruṣa is seen by ignorance as though he had parts; he is to be shown alone, by knowledge, through the removal of the parts laid on him: so the parts are said to arise from him. For in the reality that is wholly without particulars, non-dual and pure, the dealing of teaching and thing taught cannot go on without superimposition; so the arising, staying and ending of the parts, which belong to the field of ignorance, are laid on it. The parts, as they arise, stay and dissolve, are always seen as not apart from consciousness.

Śaṅkara: hence some are deluded: consciousness itself, they say, is born and perishes at every moment in the form of a pot and the like, as ghee (melts) from contact with fire. Others say that when it ceases all is as it were void. Others, that consciousness of a pot and the like, not eternal, arises and perishes in the eternal Self who is the knower. The Lokāyatikas, that consciousness is a property of the elements. (The truth is that) the Self is consciousness itself, which neither goes nor comes, and it appears with the properties of the adjuncts, name, form and the rest: so the texts ‘Brahman is truth, knowledge, the infinite’, ‘Brahman is knowing’, ‘Brahman is knowledge and bliss’, ‘a mass of knowledge only’.

Śaṅkara: while things depart from their own form, consciousness does not depart: in whatever way each thing is known, by the very fact of its being known the consciousness of it is unfailing. That something is real and is not known is not tenable, any more than that colour is seen and there is no eye. The known fails knowledge; knowledge never fails the known, for when one known thing is absent knowledge is there in another. Without knowledge there is nothing known for anyone, for in deep sleep none is seen.

Śaṅkara: objection: in deep sleep knowledge too is absent, so knowledge fails just as the known does. No: knowledge, which shows the known, reveals it as light does; as the absence of light cannot be made out from the absence of what it would reveal, so the absence of knowledge in deep sleep cannot. When the eye perceives no colour in the dark, even the nihilist cannot suppose that there is no eye. If he does suppose the absence of knowledge when the known is absent, he must say by what the absence of that knowledge is supposed by which he supposes that absence; for that absence too is a thing known and cannot be without knowledge.

Śaṅkara: objection: knowledge is not other than the known, so when the known is absent knowledge is absent. No: the nihilists hold that absence too is a thing known, and eternal; if knowledge is not other than it, knowledge would be eternal, and since that absence would have the nature of knowledge, its being an absence is a word only: in truth there is no absence and no non-eternity of knowledge, and nothing of ours is lost if the mere name ‘absence’ is laid on eternal knowledge. If absence, though known, is other than knowledge, then the absence of the known is not the absence of knowledge. If it is said that the known is other than knowledge but knowledge is not other than the known: that is words only and makes no difference; if the two are held to be one, it is like saying that vahni is other than agni but agni is not other than vahni. And if knowledge is other than the known, it is settled that knowledge is not absent when the known is absent.

Śaṅkara: objection: knowledge is absent because it is not seen when the known is absent. No: knowing is admitted in deep sleep; the nihilists themselves admit that knowledge exists then. If they say that there knowledge is known by itself: no, for the difference is established: the knowledge whose object is an absence is other than that absence which it knows, so the known and knowledge are different, and that, once established, cannot be made otherwise by a hundred nihilists, any more than a dead man can be brought to life. Objection: on your view knowledge must be known by another, and that by another, without end. No: all can be divided in two. When all is the known of someone, the knowledge that is other than it is knowledge only: this second part alone is held by those who are not nihilists, not a third that has knowledge for its object; so there is no regress. Objection: if knowledge is not known by itself, omniscience is lost. Let that fault too be his; why should we remove it? The regress is his also, since he holds knowledge to be a thing known: for the nihilists knowledge must be known, and as it cannot be known by itself the regress cannot be stopped. If he says the fault is the same for both: no, because knowledge is one. One knowledge, in all places, times, persons and states, appears as many through the many adjuncts, name, form and the rest, like the reflections of the sun in water and the like. So there is no fault; and that is what is said here.

Śaṅkara: objection: by the text ‘here within the body’ the Puruṣa is limited, like a jujube fruit in a bowl. No: he is the cause of the parts, prāṇa and the rest; one limited by the body alone could not be understood as the cause of prāṇa, faith and the other parts. And the body is an effect of the parts: the body, an effect of the parts which are effects of the Puruṣa, cannot hold within itself the cause of its cause, as a bowl holds a jujube. If it is said, as with seed and tree: the tree is the effect of the seed, and its effect, the fruit, a mango or the like, holds within it the seed, the cause of its cause: no, because there the seeds are other and because they have parts. In the example the seeds enclosed in the fruit of the tree are other than the seed that was the cause; here the very same Puruṣa, the cause of its cause, is said to be within the body. And seed, tree and the rest have parts, so they can be container and contained; the Puruṣa is without parts, while the parts and the body have them. By this even space cannot have the body for its container, much less the Puruṣa, the cause of space. If it is said, what need of an example, let it be so on the word of the text: no, a text does not make things; it does not work to make a thing other than it is, but to show it as it is. So the words ‘within the body’ are to be seen like the words ‘space is within the egg (of the world)’. And (it is said so) because the body is the place where he is perceived: by the marks of seeing, hearing, thinking, knowing and the rest the Puruṣa is perceived within the body, as though limited. Not even a fool would wish to say, even in his mind, that the cause of space is limited by the body like a jujube in a bowl; how much less the Veda, which is the authority.

Śaṅkara, going on to the next mantra: ‘in whom these sixteen parts arise’ was said to qualify the Puruṣa; in what order that arising, mentioned for another purpose, takes place is now told, and also to show that creation has a conscious being before it.

translations.text: He reflected: ‘On whose departing shall I have departed, and on whose staying shall I stay?’

notes: Śaṅkara: he, the Puruṣa of sixteen parts about whom Bhāradvāja asked, made a reflection, a seeing, about creation, its fruit, its order and the rest. How? ‘When which particular agent has departed from the body shall I have departed, and when which stays in the body shall I stay?’

translations.text: He created prāṇa; from prāṇa faith, space, air, fire, water, earth, the organs, mind and food; from food strength, austerity, the mantras, rites, the worlds, and in the worlds name.

notes: Śaṅkara: objection (of the Sāṃkhya): the Self is no agent; pradhāna is the agent, and, taking the purpose of Puruṣa as its end, acts in the form of mahat and the rest. So it is not tenable to speak of Puruṣa's acting independently after reflection, when pradhāna, the equal state of sattva and the other guṇas, established by proof, is there as the maker of creation, or the atoms that follow the will of the Lord; also because the Self, being one, has no means by which to act, and because it cannot be the doer of harm to itself: no conscious being who acts with thought would do harm to himself. So ‘he reflected’ and the rest is a figure by which unconscious pradhāna, acting in a fixed order for the purpose of Puruṣa as though after reflection, is spoken of as conscious, as a servant who does everything for the king is called king.

Śaṅkara: no: the Self can be an agent just as it can be an enjoyer. As for the Sāṃkhya the Self, though pure consciousness and unchanging, is an enjoyer, so for those who follow the Veda its making of the world after reflection is tenable, on the authority of the Veda. Objection: change into another principle is what brings non-eternity, impurity and manyness on the Self; a modification of its own nature as pure consciousness does not. So Puruṣa's being an enjoyer within himself is no fault; but for you, in the making of creation there is change into another principle, and so all the faults follow. No: for the one Self a difference made by the adjuncts of name and form, in the field of ignorance, is admitted, so that the dealings laid down by the teaching on bondage, liberation and the rest may go on; in highest truth the reality without adjuncts is one only, without a second, not to be entered by the understanding of any reasoner, fearless, auspicious; there is neither agency nor enjoyership there, nor act, means and fruit, since all things are non-dual.

Śaṅkara: the Sāṃkhyas first suppose that agency, act, means and fruit are laid on Puruṣa by ignorance; then, being outside the Veda, they take fright at that and want Puruṣa to be an enjoyer in highest truth, and suppose pradhāna to be another principle, as real as Puruṣa; so they come within reach of the other reasoners' arguments and are struck down by them, and the other reasoners by the Sāṃkhyas. Thus, supposing things that contradict one another, like animals after the same meat, they are drawn far from the truth. We say a little of the faults of the reasoners' views, not with the reasoners' zeal, but so that seekers of liberation may set those views aside and hold to the truth of the Vedānta, the vision of oneness. So it has been said: ‘leaving the cause of dispute among the disputants themselves, his right understanding kept safe from them, the knower of the Veda goes happily to peace’.

Śaṅkara: further, no difference can be shown between the two modifications, enjoying and acting. What is this modification called enjoying, of another kind than acting, by which Puruṣa is supposed to be enjoyer only and not agent, and pradhāna agent only and not enjoyer? If it is said that Puruṣa, pure consciousness, changes within himself when he enjoys, not by change into another principle, while pradhāna changes into another principle and so is many, impure and unconscious, Puruṣa being the opposite: that is no difference, only words. If the Puruṣa, pure consciousness alone before experience arises, takes on the particular called enjoyership when it arises and is pure consciousness again when it ends, then pradhāna too, having changed into mahat and the rest, comes back and stays in its own form: there is no difference in the supposition. If Puruṣa is pure consciousness even at the time of experience, as before, then experience is not truly his. If the modification of pure consciousness at that time is real and is his experience: pradhāna too is modified at that time and would be an enjoyer. If only the modification of pure consciousness is enjoyership: there is no reason why fire and the like, with properties of their own such as heat, are not enjoyers. If both enjoy together: then pradhāna's being for the sake of another fails, for two enjoyers cannot be principal and subordinate to each other, as two lights cannot light each other. If the enjoyership of the unchanging Puruṣa is the rise of a reflection of his consciousness in the mind, in which sattva prevails and to which experience belongs: then, there being no particular in Puruṣa, to suppose him an enjoyer is pointless. If Puruṣa, always without particulars, has no harm in the form of experience, for the removal of whose harm is the teaching, the means of liberation, composed? If to remove a harm laid on by ignorance: then the supposition that Puruṣa is in truth enjoyer and not agent, and pradhāna agent and not enjoyer and another thing truly real, is outside the Veda, pointless and without ground, and seekers of liberation should not regard it.

Śaṅkara: objection: if all is one, the composing of the teaching and the rest is pointless too. No, for they are not there: the question whether it is pointless or not could arise only if there were composers of the teaching and seekers of its fruit; in the oneness of the Self there are none apart from it, and without them the question cannot arise. In admitting the oneness of the Self you admit the authority for it, and that teaching says that no such question holds then: ‘where all has become his very Self, by what would he see whom?’; and it shows how the composing of the teaching holds elsewhere than in the reality, in the field of ignorance: ‘where there is duality, as it were’, at length in the Vājasaneyaka. Here too knowledge and ignorance, the higher and the lower, are set apart at the very beginning of the teaching. So the soldiers that are the reasoners' arguments cannot enter here, into the oneness of the Self, guarded by the arm of the king, the authority of the Vedānta. By this the objection that Brahman has no means for making creation is answered, for it has the differences of many powers and means, known from the Veda, made by the adjuncts of name and form that ignorance makes; and so is the objection that the Self would do harm to itself. The example of the king and the servant does not fit here, for it would set aside the primary sense of the Veda, ‘he reflected’, which is the authority: a word is taken figuratively only where its primary sense is impossible. For an unconscious thing an activity towards Puruṣa that is fixed with regard to the difference of freed and bound Puruṣas and to agent, act, place, time and cause, for the fruits of bondage and liberation, is not tenable; on the view that the all-knowing Lord is the maker, it is.

Śaṅkara: as by a lord, prāṇa, who holds every office, is created by the Puruṣa. Having reflected in the way told, he created the prāṇa of all, called Hiraṇyagarbha, the support of the organs of all living beings, the inner self. From that prāṇa, faith, the cause of all beings' turning to good action. Then the great elements, which are the seats of the means of experiencing the fruit of action: space, with sound for its quality; air, with its own quality, touch, and that of its cause, so of two qualities; fire, of three, with colour; water, of four, with taste; earth, of five, with smell. Then the organs, made of those same elements, of two kinds, for knowing and for acting, ten in number; and their lord, the mind, within, whose mark is doubt and intention. Having thus created the body and the organs of living beings, for their keeping he created food, rice, barley and the like; from food, when eaten, strength, the means of setting about every action; for those beings who have strength and become impure, austerity, the means of purifying; the mantras, Ṛc, Yajus, Sāman and those of the Atharvans and Aṅgirases, the means of rites, for those whose inner and outer organs are purified by austerity; then rites, the Agnihotra and the like; then the worlds, the fruit of rites; and in them the names of the beings created, Devadatta, Yajñadatta and so on. So these parts are created in dependence on the seed that is the faults of living beings, ignorance and the rest, like the two moons, gnats and flies created by the sight of one whose eyes are diseased, or like all the things created by a dreamer; and they dissolve again in that same Puruṣa, leaving the division of name, form and the rest.
The e-text reads chadvāṃ; it is set right here to chraddhāṃ, as the bhāṣya has it.

sanskrit.deva:
स यथेमा नद्यः स्यन्दमानाः समुद्रायणाः समुद्रं प्राप्यास्तं गच्छन्ति ।
भिद्येते तासां नामरूपे ।
समुद्र इत्येवं प्रोच्यते ।
एवमेवास्य परिद्रष्टुरिमाः षोडश कलाः पुरुषायणाः पुरुषं प्राप्यास्तं गच्छन्ति ।
भिद्येते चासां नामरूपे ।
पुरुष इत्येवं प्रोच्यते ।
स एषोऽकलोऽमृतो भवति ।
तदेष श्लोकः ॥ ५ ॥

padaccheda.deva: सः यथा इमाः नद्यः स्यन्दमानाः समुद्र-अयणाः समुद्रम् प्राप्य अस्तम् गच्छन्ति भिद्येते तासाम् नाम-रूपे समुद्रः इति एवम् प्रोच्यते एवम् एव अस्य परिद्रष्टुः इमाः षोडश कलाः पुरुष-अयणाः पुरुषम् प्राप्य अस्तम् गच्छन्ति भिद्येते च आसाम् नाम-रूपे पुरुषः इति एवम् प्रोच्यते सः एषः अकलः अमृतः भवति तत् एषः श्लोकः

translations.text: As these flowing rivers, whose goal is the sea, on reaching the sea go to their setting, their name and form are broken up, and it is called simply ‘the sea’: just so these sixteen parts of this seer of all, whose goal is the Puruṣa, on reaching the Puruṣa go to their setting, their name and form are broken up, and it is called simply ‘the Puruṣa’. He (who knows thus) becomes without parts and deathless. On this there is this verse:

notes: Śaṅkara: this is the example. The rivers have the sea for their goal, for their very self; on reaching it they go to their setting, the hiding of name and form. Their names and forms, Gaṅgā, Yamunā and so on, perish; when these are gone the thing, which is water, is called ‘the sea’. So with this Puruṣa, the matter in hand: paridraṣṭuḥ, the seer all round, the maker of the seeing that is his own nature, as the sun is the maker on every side of the light that is itself. The sixteen parts, prāṇa and the rest, have the Puruṣa for their goal, as the rivers the sea; reaching him, becoming one with his self, they set in the same way. Their names, prāṇa and so on, and their several forms are broken up; and when name and form are broken up, the reality that has not perished is called ‘the Puruṣa’ by the knowers of Brahman.

Śaṅkara: one who knows thus, to whom the teacher has shown the way of the dissolving of the parts, becomes without parts when the parts, prāṇa and the rest, born of ignorance, desire and action, have been dissolved by knowledge. Death is caused by the parts that ignorance makes; when they are gone, being without parts he becomes deathless.
The e-text has the word katham before the mantra; it belongs to the bhāṣya and is left out here.

words.meaning: in the hub of a chariot wheel

grammar.en: past passive participle f. nom. pl.

translations.text: ‘Know that Puruṣa who is to be known, in whom the parts are set like the spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel, so that death may not afflict you.’

notes: Śaṅkara: as the spokes, set in the hub of the chariot wheel, rest on it, so the parts, prāṇa and the rest, are set in the Puruṣa at the times of arising, staying and dissolving. That Puruṣa, the self of the parts, called puruṣa because he is full or because he lies in the city, is to be known. veda: one should know. ‘So that, pupils, death may not afflict you’: if the Puruṣa is not known you remain in pain, fallen into the affliction that death causes; let that not be yours.

sanskrit.deva:
तान्होवाच ।
एतावदेवाहमेतत्परं ब्रह्म वेद ।
नातः परमस्तीति ॥ ७ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
tān hovāca |
etāvad evāham etat paraṃ brahma veda |
nātaḥ param astīti || 7 ||

lines.iast: etāvad evāham etat paraṃ brahma veda

padaccheda.iast: tān ha uvāca etāvat eva aham etat param brahma veda na ataḥ param asti iti
padaccheda.deva: तान् ह उवाच एतावत् एव अहम् एतत् परम् ब्रह्म वेद न अतः परम् अस्ति इति

translations.text: He said to them: ‘Thus far only do I know this supreme Brahman; there is nothing higher than this.’

notes: Śaṅkara: having taught the pupils thus, Pippalāda said: this much only is the supreme Brahman that is to be known; there is nothing higher than it to be known. He said so to remove the pupils' doubt that something unknown might remain, and to give them the conviction that they had gained their end.

sanskrit.deva:
ते तमर्चयन्तस्त्वं हि नः पिता योऽस्माकमविद्यायाः परं पारं तारयसीति ।
नमः परमऋषिभ्यो नमः परमऋषिभ्यः ॥ ८ ॥

translations.text: They, honouring him, (said): ‘You indeed are our father, who take us across to the farther shore of ignorance.’ Homage to the supreme seers! Homage to the supreme seers!

notes: Śaṅkara: the pupils, taught by the teacher and having gained their end, seeing no price that could be paid for the knowledge, honoured him by strewing handfuls of flowers at his feet and bowing their heads. ‘You are our father’, since by knowledge you have begotten the body that is Brahman, eternal, ageless, deathless, fearless; you take us by the raft of knowledge across the great ocean of ignorance, of wrong knowledge, with its sea-beasts, birth, old age, death, disease and pain, to the other shore, called liberation, from which there is no return. So fatherhood towards us is more fitly yours than another's: the other father begets the body only, and yet he is the most to be honoured in the world; what need be said of one who gives fearlessness without end? ‘Homage to the supreme seers’, the founders of the tradition of the knowledge of Brahman; the repetition is to show reverence.
